extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, students of fiction, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on composing novels with attention to the relation between character and situation, how to make characters live in art, choose and balance novel forms, and handle dialogue, selection, and scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity of the artist / transmutation into art
rubrics_metrics.description: “The business of the artist is to make weep, and not to weep, to make laugh, and not to laugh; and unless tears and laughter, and flesh-and-blood, are transmuted by him into the substance that art works in, they are nothing to his purpose, or to ours.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotional material (tears, laughter, real-life detail) must be transformed by the artist into the medium of art rather than simply reproduced as autobiography or raw feeling. Anti-pattern: assuming personal/real tears or spectacle alone constitute artistic success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft must be learned: find rules and formulas at execution
rubrics_metrics.description: “The creatures of that fourth-dimensional world are born as helpless as the human animal; and each time the artist passes from dream to execution he will need to find the rules and formulas on the threshold.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even writers who seem to have innate power must acquire techniques and formal rules to render their visions effectively; treat artistry as skill plus vision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: novel of situation vs novel of character and manners
rubrics_metrics.description: “In [a novel of situation], the persons imagined by the author almost always spring out of a vision of the situation, and are inevitably conditioned by it... whereas in [the novel of character and manners], the author’s characters are first born, and then mysteriously proceed to work out their own destinies.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose whether your primary organizing principle is a compelling situation (drama-driven) or character (people-driven). Many subjects can be treated either way; know which you're aiming for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of puppet-characters in novels of situation
rubrics_metrics.description: “The novel of situation... seizes the characters in its steely grip, and jiu-jitsus them into the required attitude... central characters tend to be the least real... survivors of the old ‘hero’ and ‘heroine’ ... mere projections of [the author].”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a situation is dominant, take care characters do not become mere instruments of plot. Anti-patterns: protagonists who only do what the plot needs (turning to 'sawdust' or 'puppets').

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters should be both typical and individual; universal and particular
rubrics_metrics.description: “The novelist’s permanent problem is that of making his people at once typical and individual, universal and particular...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to create characters who embody wider human truths while retaining specific individuality—avoid caricature or mere archetype.

rubrics_metrics.name: When situation precedes character, delay finalizing the situation until characters emerge
rubrics_metrics.description: “When the problem comes to the novelist before he sees the characters engaged in it, he must be all the more deliberate... must let it lie in his mind till it brings forth of itself the kind of people who would naturally be involved in that particular plight.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you conceive your tale as a situation, incubate it until the right characters form who would naturally belong in it, rather than forcing pre-made characters into a contrived predicament.

rubrics_metrics.name: The tuning-fork of truth: ask what characters would make of the situation
rubrics_metrics.description: “The writer must... bear in mind... that his business is not to ask what the situation would be likely to make of his characters, but what his characters, being what they are, would make of the situation. This question, which is the tuning-fork of truth...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always test scenes and dialogue against the question: would these characters, given their traits, actually behave/speak this way in this situation? Use this test to preserve reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue must reflect character, not the needs of the situation
rubrics_metrics.description: “The moment the novelist finds that his characters are talking not as they naturally would, but as the situation requires... his effect has been produced at the expense of reality...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let dialogue spring from character motivation and voice; avoid writing lines solely because they advance the plot. Anti-pattern: speeches that feel like authorial convenience rather than character speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid interlarding crucial dialogue with irrelevant small-talk
rubrics_metrics.description: “Some novelists... have tried to turn [the danger] by interlarding these crucial dialogues with irrelevant small-talk... But this is to fall again into the trap of... ‘a reality in nature which is not one in art.’”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not fake realism by padding intense scenes with gratuitous chit-chat. Selection and purposeful speech are superior to mimicking ‘real’ conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instinct (and art) of selection
rubrics_metrics.description: “His characters must talk as they would in reality, and yet everything not relevant to his tale must be eliminated. The secret of success lies in his instinct of selection.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editing/selection is central: include only what illuminates character or advances the design. Train the instinct to cut irrelevant material even if it 'feels' real.

rubrics_metrics.name: Even novels of character require situation/climax
rubrics_metrics.description: “Even the novel of character and manners can never be without situation, that is, without some sort of climax caused by the contending forces engaged.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regardless of form, a novel needs a central predicament or conflict producing a climax; complacent 'slice-of-life' must still select and shape toward completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stream-of-consciousness/slice-of-life still involves selection and stylization
rubrics_metrics.description: “The ‘stream of consciousness’ — which is simply the ‘slice-of-life’ of the ’eighties renamed — ... contains its own condemnation, since every attempt to employ it of necessity involves selection, and selection in the long run must eventually lead to the transposition, the ‘stylization,’ of the subject.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using apparent spontaneity, be conscious that you are selecting and stylizing; do not excuse lack of structure by calling it realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overemphasizing trivial incidents unless they illustrate a general law
rubrics_metrics.description: “The incident, insignificant in itself, must illustrate some general law, and turn on some deep movement of the soul. If the novelist wants to hang his drama on a button, let it at least be one of Lear’s.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small incidents can be powerful only if they illuminate a profound human truth; triviality for its own sake weakens the novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of methods: combine character, situation, manners, and social background in due proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is a matter for the novelist’s genius to combine all these ingredients in their due proportion; and then we shall have ‘Emma’ or ‘The Egoist’... ‘War and Peace,’ ‘Vanity Fair’... if all the points of view and all the methods are to be harmonized in the achievement of a great picture wherein the individual, the group and their social background have each a perfectly apportioned share...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for appropriate scale and proportion across elements; great novels harmonize multiple methods rather than adhere dogmatically to one.

rubrics_metrics.name: The novelist needs range, richness, and solidity when situation dominates
rubrics_metrics.description: “The tendency of the situation to take hold of the novelist’s imagination... can be resisted only by richness and solidity of temperament. The writer must have a range wide enough to include... all the inconsequences of human desire, ambition, cruelty, weakness and sublimity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you are driven by a powerful situation, cultivate a broad emotional and imaginative range so characters remain complex and human under pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making central characters mere expressions of the author’s convictions
rubrics_metrics.description: “These characters... are his in the sense of tending to do and say what he would do, or imagines he would do, in given circumstances, and being mere projections of his own personality they lack the substance and relief of the minor characters...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep authorial bias out of protagonists' inner lives; give them autonomy, quirks, and flaws distinct from the author's persona.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary artistic test: make your people live
rubrics_metrics.description: “Out of all the flux of judgments... the quality the greatest novelists have always had in common is that of making their people live.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Above technique or virtuosity, aim for vivacity and life in characterization; living characters have the greatest chance of surviving reader memory and critical judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use experimental technique in service of purposive conduct and unity
rubrics_metrics.description: On Proust: though he probes 'half-conscious states... obscure associations of thought' he 'never loses himself... the object is always to report the conscious, purposive conduct of his characters' and he attains unity by selection and design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you employ long, experimental, or digressive methods, ensure they serve to reveal purposeful behavior and contribute to an overall unity; avoid indulgent fragmentation that lacks design.
